Representation of a
crontab expression
that can calculate the next time it matches.
{@code CronExpression} instances are created through
{@link #parse(String)}; the next match is determined with
{@link #next(Temporal)}.
Parse the given
crontab expression
string into a {@code CronExpression}.
The string has six single space-separated time and date fields:
The following rules apply:
<li>
The "day of month" field can be {@code nW}, which stands for "the nearest
weekday to day of the month {@code n}".
If {@code n} falls on Saturday, this yields the Friday before it.
If {@code n} falls on Sunday, this yields the Monday after,
which also happens if {@code n} is {@code 1} and falls on a Saturday
(i.e. {@code 1W} stands for "the first weekday of the month").
<li>
The "day of week" field can be {@code d#n} (or {@code DDD#n}), which
stands for "the {@code n}-th day of week {@code d} (or {@code DDD}) in
the month".

A trigger for periodic task execution. The period may be applied as either
fixed-rate or fixed-delay, and an initial delay value may also be configured.
The default initial delay is 0, and the default behavior is fixed-delay
(i.e. the interval between successive executions is measured from each
completion time). To measure the interval between the
scheduled start time of each execution instead, set the
'fixedRate' property to {@code true}.
Note that the TaskScheduler interface already defines methods for scheduling
tasks at fixed-rate or with fixed-delay. Both also support an optional value
for the initial delay. Those methods should be used directly whenever
possible. The value of this Trigger implementation is that it can be used
within components that rely on the Trigger abstraction. For example, it may
be convenient to allow periodic triggers, cron-based triggers, and even
custom Trigger implementations to be used interchangeably.
